source_text: Οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱ πόλεις μόνον, οὐδὲ αἱ χῶραι, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἰκίαι πολλάκις καθ' ἑαυτὰς ἐμάχοντο· καὶ παντὸς ἐμφυλίου πολέμου χαλεπώτερος ἦν ὁ τότε κατέχων θόρυβος. Καὶ γὰρ καὶ χρήματα ἀνηρπάζετο, καὶ ἐλευθερία προεδίδοτο, καὶ περὶ αὐτῆς τῆς ζωῆς ὁ κίνδυνος ἐπεκρέματο, οὐχὶ βαρβάρων ἐπιτρεχόντων καὶ ἐπηρεαζόντων, ἀλλ' αὐτῶν τῶν δοκούντων προεστάναι καὶ ἄρχειν, πολεμίων ἁπάντων χαλεπώτερον τοὺς ἀρχομένους διατιθέντων. Καὶ τοῦτο δηλῶν ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν, ὅτι Πολλὴν ἄθλησιν ὑπεμείνατε παθημάτων· τοῦτο μὲν, ὀνειδισμοῖς τε καὶ θλίψεσι θεατριζόμενοι, τοῦτο δὲ, κοινωνοὶ τῶν οὕτως ἀναστρεφομένων γενηθέντες. Καὶ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου συνεπαθήσατε, καὶ τὴν ἁρπαγὴν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὑμῖν μετὰ χαρᾶς προσεδέξασθε. Καὶ Γαλάταις δέ φησι· Τοσαῦτα ἐπάθετε εἰκῆ, εἴ γε καὶ εἰκῆ. Καὶ Θεσσαλονικεῦσι δὲ, καὶ Φιλιππησίοις, καὶ πᾶσιν ἁπλῶς οἷς ἐπιστέλλει, πολλὰ τοιαῦτα μαρτυρεῖ. Καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον ἦν τὸ χαλεπὸν, ὅτι πολὺς ὁ πόλεμος ἔξωθεν κεκίνητο καὶ διηνεκὴς, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῖς πιστοῖς συνέβαινε γίνεσθαί τινα σκάνδαλα καὶ ἔρεις καὶ φιλονεικίας καὶ ζηλοτυπίας· καὶ ταῦτα αὐτὰ δηλῶν ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν· Ἔξωθεν μάχαι, ἔσωθεν φόβοι. Καὶ οὗτος ἐκείνου χαλεπώτερος ὁ πόλεμος ἦν, καὶ τοῖς ἀρχομένοις καὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις. Οὐχ οὕτω γοῦν τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἐδεδοίκει τὰς ἐπιβουλὰς ὁ Παῦλος, ὡς τὰ ἔνδον πτώματα, καὶ τὰς τῶν οἰκείων παρανομίας. Ὅτε γοῦν ἐπόρνευσέ τις παρὰ Κορινθίοις, ἅπαντα τὸν χρόνον ἐκεῖνον πενθῶν διετέλεσε, τὰ σπλάγχνα σπαράττων τὰ ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ πικρὸν ὀλολύζων. Ἦν τι καὶ τρίτον οὐκ ἔλαττον τῶν εἰρημένων, πολὺν ἐπάγον τοῖς πιστεύουσι πόνον, αὐτὴ τῶν πρα50.421 γμάτων ἡ φύσις πολλῶν ἱδρώτων γέμουσα καὶ πόνων. Οὐ γὰρ εὔκολος καὶ ῥᾳδία τις ἦν ἡ ὁδὸς, ἐφ' ἣν ἦγον αὐτοὺς οἱ ἀπόστολοι, ἀλλὰ τραχεῖα καὶ δυσκατόρθωτος καὶ φιλοσόφου τινὸς καὶ ἀγρύπνου δεομένη ψυχῆς καὶ ἠκριβωμένης πανταχόθεν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς στενὴν καὶ τεθλιμμένην αὐτὴν ἐκάλεσεν. Οὐ γὰρ ἐξῆν ἀδεῶς ζῇν, καθάπερ παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν, ἐν αἰσχρότητι καὶ μέθῃ καὶ ἀδδηφαγίᾳ καὶ τρυφῇ καὶ πολυτελείᾳ· ἀλλ' ἔδει καὶ θυμὸν χαλινοῦν, καὶ ἐπιθυμίας ἀτόπου κρατεῖν, καὶ χρημάτων ὑπερορᾷν, καὶ δόξαν καταπατεῖν, καὶ φθόνου καὶ βασκανίας ἀνώτερον εἶναι. Ταῦτα δὲ ἡλίκον πόνον παρέχει, ἴσασιν οἱ καθ' ἡμέραν αὐτοῖς πυκτεύοντες. Τί γὰρ ἐπιθυμίας ἀτόπου χαλεπώτερον εἰπέ μοι, ἣ, καθάπερ κύων λυττῶν, συνεχῶς ἡμῖν ἐπιπηδᾷ, καὶ καθ' ἡμέραν ἡμῖν διενοχλεῖ, καὶ δεῖται διηνεκῶς ἐγρηγορυίας ψυχῆς; Τί δὲ καὶ ὀργῆς πικρότερον; Γλυκὺ μὲν γὰρ τὸ τὸν ἠδικηκότα ἀμύνασθαι, ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐξῆν. Καὶ τί λέγω, τὸν ἠδικηκότα οὐκ ἐξῆν ἀμύνασθαι; Εὐεργετεῖν ἔδει τοὺς λυποῦντας, καὶ εὐλογεῖν τοὺς λοιδορουμένους, καὶ μηδὲ ῥῆμα πικρὸν ἐκβάλλειν ποτέ· καὶ σωφροσύνην δὲ, οὐ τὴν μέχρι τῶν ἔργων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν μέχρι τῆς ἐννοίας ἐπιδείκνυσθαι ἔδει. Οὐ γὰρ μόνον αὐτῆς τῆς ἀκολάστου πράξεως, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὄψεως τῆς τοιαύτης ἀπέχεσθαι δεῖ, καὶ μηδὲ ἐντρυφᾷν ταῖς ὄψεσι τῶν εὐμόρφων γυναικῶν, ὡς καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς θεωρίας ταύτης τὴν ἐσχάτην μέλλοντας ὑποστήσεσθαι δίκην. Ἐπεὶ οὖν πολὺς ὁ πόλεμος ἦν παρὰ τῶν ἔξωθεν, πολὺς ὁ φόβος παρὰ τῶν ἔνδοθεν, πολὺς ὁ πόνος ὁ πρὸς τὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐργασίαν.
thought_title: The threefold war against the first believers
orientation: Chrysostom is describing how hard the first Christians had it, before he shows why Paul kept teaching the resurrection to encourage them.
pass_a_gloss: For not only the cities, not only the regions, but also households often fought by themselves; and the turmoil then prevailing was harsher than every civil war. For both property was being snatched away, and freedom was being betrayed, and the danger hung over life itself, not with barbarians running in and abusing them, but with the very men who seemed to stand before and rule treating the ruled more harshly than all enemies. And Paul, making this clear, said: You endured a great contest of sufferings; on the one hand, being made a spectacle by reproaches and afflictions, on the other hand, having become partners of those who were so treated. For you also suffered together with my bonds, and you accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy. And to the Galatians he says: You suffered so many things in vain, if indeed also in vain. And to the Thessalonians, and to the Philippians, and simply to all to whom he writes, he bears witness to many such things. And not only this was the hard thing, that the war from outside was stirred up great and continuous, but that also among the faithful themselves it happened that certain scandals and strifes and rivalries and jealousies arose; and Paul, making these very things clear, said: Battles outside, fears within. And this war was harsher than that one, both for the ruled and for the teachers. Paul did not so much fear the plots of enemies as the falls within and the transgressions of his own people. When someone committed fornication among the Corinthians, he spent all that time mourning, tearing his own inward parts, and wailing bitterly. There was also a third thing not less than the things mentioned, bringing much toil upon the believers, the very nature of affairs being full of many sweats and labors. For the road onto which the apostles were leading them was not easy and light, but rough and hard to set right and requiring a philosophic and wakeful soul and one made exact from every side. For this reason also Christ called it narrow and afflicted. For it was not permitted to live fearlessly, as among the Greeks, in shamefulness and drunkenness and gluttony and luxury and extravagance; but it was necessary both to bridle anger, and to master disordered desire, and to despise money, and to trample on glory, and to be above envy and malice. And how much toil these things bring, those who box with them daily know. For what is harsher than disordered desire, tell me, which, like a raging dog, constantly leaps upon us, and troubles us daily, and needs a perpetually wakeful soul? And what is more bitter than anger? For sweet it is to defend oneself against the one who has wronged, but this was not permitted. And why do I say, it was not permitted to defend oneself against the one who has wronged? It was necessary to do good to those who grieve, and to bless those who revile, and never to cast out a bitter word; and it was necessary to display self-control, not only that which goes as far as deeds, but also that which goes as far as thought. For not only from the licentious act itself, but also from such a gaze it is necessary to abstain, and not even to feast the eyes on the sights of beautiful women, as those who are about to undergo the final punishment even for this looking. Since therefore the war from those outside was great, the fear from those within was great, the toil toward the working of virtue was great.

Glossary term; keeps the pressure/trouble sense of the Greek rather than a more general 'troubles'.
Renders the violent seizure of property in the Hebrews quotation literally, matching the source's concrete noun.
Keeps the stark Pauline antithesis 'outside...within' and the plural 'fears' exactly.

Keeps the Matthean wording literally; 'afflicted' matches the glossary term for θλῖψις.

pass_b_english: For it was not only cities and countrysides that fought, but often households fought against themselves, and the turmoil that gripped them then was harsher than any civil war. Property was being snatched away, freedom was being betrayed, and danger hung over life itself—not because barbarians were raiding and attacking, but because the very people who seemed to be leaders and rulers treated their subjects more harshly than any enemy. Paul made this clear when he said, “You endured a great contest of sufferings: sometimes being made a spectacle through reproaches and afflictions, and sometimes becoming partners with those who were treated this way. For you suffered together with me in my chains, and you accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy” (Hebrews 10:32-34). And to the Galatians he says, “Did you suffer so many things in vain, if indeed it was in vain?” (Galatians 3:4). And to the Thessalonians, and the Philippians, and simply to all those to whom he writes, he bears witness to many such things.

And this was not the only difficulty—that a great and unceasing war was stirred up from outside—but also among the faithful themselves there happened to be scandals, strifes, rivalries, and jealousies. Paul made this clear when he said, “Outside are battles, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5). And this war was harsher than the other, both for those being led and for the teachers. Paul did not fear the plots of enemies as much as he feared the falls within and the transgressions of his own people. When someone among the Corinthians committed fornication, he spent all that time mourning, tearing at his own heart and crying out bitterly.

There was also a third thing, no less than those already mentioned, that brought great labor upon the faithful: the very nature of the matters themselves, full of many sweats and toils. For the road onto which the apostles led them was not easy and smooth, but rough and hard to set right, requiring a soul that was philosophical, wakeful, and precise in every way. This is why Christ called it narrow and afflicted. For it was not permitted to live without fear, as among the Greeks, in shamefulness, drunkenness, gluttony, luxury, and extravagance. Instead, one had to bridle anger, master disordered desire, look down on money, trample on glory, and rise above envy and malice. How much labor these things require is known by those who wrestle with them every day.

Tell me, what is harsher than disordered desire, which leaps on us constantly like a rabid dog, troubles us every day, and requires a soul that is perpetually awake? And what is more bitter than anger? For it is sweet to take revenge on the one who wronged you, but this was not permitted. And why do I say it was not permitted to take revenge on the one who wronged you? One had to do good to those who caused grief, bless those who insulted, and never utter a bitter word. And one had to display self-control not only in actions but even in thought. For one must abstain not only from the licentious act itself but also from such looking, and not even feast one's eyes on the sight of beautiful women, since one was about to undergo the ultimate punishment even for this gazing. Since, then, the war from outside was great, the fear from within was great, and the labor for the work of virtue was great.

last_rejected.why: The quotation matches Hebrews 10:32-34, but Chrysostom attributes it to Paul, and the work brief notes Pauline epistles. Hebrews is anonymous and not Pauline in modern scholarship, but Chrysostom considered it Pauline. However, the work brief specifies 'Pauline epistles' and lists Hebrews separately not under Paul's sections. The citation is technically correct for the words but may misrepresent authorship as understood in the brief.
last_rejected.ruling: Source says ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν; Chrysostom attributes Hebrews to Paul. Citation Hebrews 10:32-34 is correct; no error.
